To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) the acquisition of the syntactic properties of CLLD and fronting are independent; b) semantic knowledge of CLLD is acquired early and independently of syntactic knowledge of clitic doubling; c) discourse knowledge of CLLD and of fronting are not acquired by intermediate speakers, and are acquired by advanced speakers.

(a) all learners are sensitive (i.e. they know) to the semantic constraints of CLLD and fronted focus; (b) the near-native speakers have native-like discourse knowledge of CLLD and of the relationship between the fronted focus and the antecedents; (c) the advanced speakers have partial discourse knowledge of CLLDs; and (d) the intermediate speakers have no evidence of discourse knowledge.

(1) all learners were sensitive to the semantic relationship between the discourse antecedent and the anaphor; (2) the near-native speakers demonstrated native-like discourse knowledge; (3) the advanced speakers displayed some knowledge of discourse; (4) the intermediate speakers did not display any knowledge of discourse; and (5) all learners displayed native-like syntactic knowledge of clitic left dislocated constructions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether L2 acquisition is a gradual process or not, with respect to the acquisition of syntax–discourse interfaces.
the question: What are the factors that contribute to successful acquisition at the interface between syntax and discourse?
the acquisition of the syntax–discursive interface and how it is affected by L2 experience.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

while the advanced speakers are able to process the semantic constraints of the constructions of clitic left dislocations and fronted focus, they have not acquired the pragmatic features of the constructions.
the advanced and intermediate speakers are not yet at the syntax– discourse interface, while the near-native speakers have successfully acquired this interface.
the advanced learners are at the syntax–semantics interface, and the intermediate speakers at the syntax–phonology interface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Interface Hypotheses is a useful tool for explaining L2 acquisition, but that it needs to be modified to account for all the factors involved.
the advanced and near-native learners have acquired the syntax–discours interface, but the intermediate learners have not.
acquisition of syntax–discourse interfaces is not only possible, but also possible to achieve at a near-native level.
The main takeaway from our work is that
acquisition of the syntax–discurse interface is not necessarily the last to be acquired.
the interface is a fruitful area of research for SLA.
successful acquisition of discourse knowledge is possible even when the learners are not native-like in their syntactic knowledge.
